subject: Math
title: Algebra
sub: Expanding and factorising, equations, quadratics, inequalities, formulae and sequences
strategyIntro: Extended Maths is two papers of equal weight: Paper 2 (2 hours, 100 marks, no calculator) and Paper 4 (2 hours, 100 marks, calculator). Your school test may be shorter, but it is marked the same way: M marks for a correct method, A marks for the correct answer that follows, B marks for a correct result on its own.

strategy.title: Timing
points: About 1.2 minutes per mark: a 5-mark question is worth about 6 minutes.
If a question has taken twice its time, leave a gap and come back at the end.
Keep 10 minutes at the end to check answers against the question.

strategy.title: Show your working
points: Most marks are method marks. A wrong answer with clear working can still score most of the marks.
Write the calculation you are doing before the answer, e.g. 360 ÷ 12 = 30.
An answer with no working can score zero if it is wrong, and sometimes even if it is right ("show that").

strategy.title: Paper 2: no calculator
points: Practise fractions, negative numbers, standard form and surds by hand.
Leave answers exact when you can: fractions, surds, or in terms of π.
Check with a quick estimate: is the answer about the right size?

strategy.title: Paper 4: calculator
points: Give answers to 3 significant figures unless the question says otherwise; angles to 1 decimal place.
Never round partway through. Keep the full value in the calculator memory (or write 4+ figures).
Use the π button, not 3.14. Check the calculator is in degrees.

strategy.title: Answer the question
points: Read the last line again: units, form of answer ("in its simplest form", "in terms of π"), and accuracy.
"Show that" questions: every step must be written, ending with the given result.
When the question says "hence", use the previous part.

commandWords: Calculate
Work out from given facts. Show the working; usually a calculator is allowed.
Work out / Find
Get the answer by any correct method. Show working.
Write down
The answer needs little or no working: you can often read or state it.
Show that
The answer is given. Write every step clearly so the examiner can follow the logic to it.
Estimate
Round each number (usually to 1 significant figure) and calculate a rough value.
Simplify
Write in its simplest form: collect like terms, cancel common factors.
Factorise (completely)
Write as a product of factors. Completely means take out every common factor.
Expand
Multiply out the brackets.
Solve
Find the value(s) of the unknown that make the equation or inequality true.
Sketch
Show the shape and key features (intercepts, turning points), not plotted accurately.
Describe fully
For a transformation: name it and give every detail (centre, angle, direction, scale factor, vector or mirror line).
Hence
Use the result you have just found to answer this part.
Give your answer in its simplest form
Cancel fractions and ratios fully; simplify surds.
quizIntro: Quick calculations and concept checks. Do each one on paper first, then pick. The wrong options are common mistakes, so if you got one, read the working in the explanation.
flashIntro: Methods, rules and formulas. Say the rule out loud (or write it down) with an example before you tap, then check you remembered every step.

flashcards.back: Multiply every term inside by the term outside: 3x(2x − 5) = 6x² − 15x. Watch signs: −2(x − 4) = −2x + 8.
Multiply every term by every term (four products), then collect like terms: (x + 3)(x − 5) = x² − 5x + 3x − 15 = x² − 2x − 15.
Expand two of the brackets first, simplify, then multiply the result by the third bracket.
Take out the HCF of the numbers and of each letter: 6x²y − 9xy² = 3xy(2x − 3y). Factorise completely means nothing common is left inside.
Find two numbers that multiply to c and add to b: x² + 7x + 12 = (x + 3)(x + 4).
Find two numbers that multiply to ac and add to b; split the middle term and group. 2x² + 7x + 3: ac = 6 → 6 and 1: 2x² + 6x + x + 3 = 2x(x + 3) + 1(x + 3) = (2x + 1)(x + 3).
Pair the terms and factorise each pair so a bracket repeats: ax + ay + bx + by = a(x + y) + b(x + y) = (a + b)(x + y).
Use brackets. If x = −3: x² = (−3)² = 9, but −x² = −9, and 2x³ = 2 × (−27) = −54.
Expand brackets, collect the x terms on one side and numbers on the other, then divide. Do the same to both sides.
Multiply every term by the LCM of the denominators: x/3 + x/4 = 7 → 4x + 3x = 84 → x = 12.
Multiply so one letter has the same coefficient in both. Same signs: subtract. Different signs: add. Solve, then substitute back to find the other letter.
Rearrange one equation (e.g. y = …) and substitute into the other. Best when one equation is already y = …

flashcards.front: One linear and one quadratic equation
flashcards.back: Substitute the linear one into the quadratic, rearrange to = 0, solve. Then find the matching value of the other letter for EACH solution: two pairs (x, y).
Let x = the unknown. Write each quantity in terms of x, form the equation, solve, then answer the actual question in context.
The solution is the point where the two graphs intersect.
Substitute your values into the ORIGINAL equations (both of them for simultaneous).
Rearrange to = 0, factorise, then set each bracket equal to 0. (x − 4)(x + 2) = 0 → x = 4 or x = −2.
For ax² + bx + c = 0: x = (−b ± √(b² − 4ac)) ÷ 2a.

flashcards.front: When should you use the quadratic formula?
flashcards.back: When it will not factorise, or when the question asks for answers to 2 d.p. or 3 s.f. (that is a hint the roots are not whole numbers).
y = (x + p)² + q has a minimum (turning) point at (−p, q).
Take a out of the x² and x terms first: 2x² + 12x + 5 = 2(x² + 6x) + 5 = 2[(x + 3)² − 9] + 5 = 2(x + 3)² − 13.

flashcards.front: Why not divide x² = 5x by x?
flashcards.back: You lose the solution x = 0. Instead: x² − 5x = 0 → x(x − 5) = 0 → x = 0 or x = 5.

flashcards.front: Quadratics from area or length problems
flashcards.back: Write the area expression, set it equal to the value, rearrange to = 0 and solve. Reject a negative length and say why.
Same as an equation, BUT if you multiply or divide both sides by a negative number, reverse the inequality sign: −2x < 6 → x > −3.
Open (empty) circle for < or >; filled circle for ≤ or ≥.
−1, 0, 1, 2, 3 (−2 is not included, 3 is).
Do the same to all three parts: 3 < 2x + 1 ≤ 9 → 2 < 2x ≤ 8 → 1 < x ≤ 4.
Solid line for ≤ or ≥ (points on the line included); broken (dashed) line for < or >.
Test a point not on the line, such as (0, 0). If it satisfies the inequality, it is on the wanted side. y > mx + c is above the line.
Read the question: Cambridge often asks you to shade the UNWANTED region so the required region R is left unshaded.

flashcards.front: Maximum or minimum of an expression in a region
flashcards.back: Check the points in the region (usually the vertices, or integer points near them) and work out the expression for each.
Undo the operations on the new subject in reverse order, doing the same to both sides.
Get all terms with the subject on one side, factorise it out, then divide: ax + b = cx + d → x(a − c) = d − b → x = (d − b)/(a − c).
Isolate the square root, then square both sides.
Isolate the squared term, then square root both sides (± if both signs are possible): A = πr² → r = √(A/π).
Factorise top and bottom fully, then cancel common brackets. Never cancel single terms from a sum.
Use a common denominator: 2/x + 3/(x + 1) = [2(x + 1) + 3x] / [x(x + 1)] = (5x + 2)/[x(x + 1)].
Factorise everything; for ÷, flip the second fraction; cancel; then multiply.

flashcards.front: Solving an equation with algebraic fractions
flashcards.back: Multiply every term by the common denominator to clear the fractions, then solve (often a quadratic).

flashcards.front: nth term of a linear sequence
flashcards.back: Common difference d → dn + (first term − d). 5, 8, 11, … → 3n + 2.

flashcards.front: nth term of a quadratic sequence
flashcards.back: Second differences are constant and equal 2a, so start with an². Subtract an² from each term and find the linear nth term of what is left; add the two parts.

flashcards.front: Is a number a term of the sequence?
flashcards.back: Set the nth term equal to the number and solve. If n is a positive whole number, it is a term; otherwise it is not.
Multiply by the same ratio r each time. nth term = a × rⁿ⁻¹, where a is the first term. 3, 6, 12, … → 3 × 2ⁿ⁻¹.
Compare with the cube numbers 1, 8, 27, 64, … e.g. 2, 9, 28, 65, … is n³ + 1.
Term-to-term: how to get the next term (e.g. add 4). Position-to-term: the nth term formula, used to find any term directly.
Squares n²: 1, 4, 9, 16, … Triangular n(n + 1)/2: 1, 3, 6, 10, 15, …

flashcards.front: Generating terms from an nth term
flashcards.back: Substitute n = 1, 2, 3, … For the 20th term substitute n = 20.

quiz.why: (2x − 3)(2x − 3) = 4x² − 6x − 6x + 9 = 4x² − 12x + 9. Squaring each term separately misses the middle term.
HCF of 12 and 18 is 6; a and b are both common: 6ab(2a − 3b). The others still have a common factor inside.
Need two numbers multiplying to −20 and adding to −1: −5 and +4.

quiz.q: Find the value of 3a² − 2b when a = −2 and b = 3.

quiz.why: ac = −24: −12 and +2. 3x² − 12x + 2x − 8 = 3x(x − 4) + 2(x − 4) = (3x + 2)(x − 4). Expand to check: middle term −12x + 2x = −10x.
Difference of two squares: 49 = 7² and 4y² = (2y)², so (7 − 2y)(7 + 2y).
5x − 10 = 3x + 4 → 2x = 14 → x = 7. Forgetting to multiply the 2 by 5 gives x = 3.
Multiply both sides by 3: 2x + 1 = 15 → 2x = 14 → x = 7.
Add (different signs on y): 3x = 12 → x = 4. Then 4 − y = 1 → y = 3. Check: 8 + 3 = 11 ✓.
Same sign on 3x, so subtract: 6y = 18 → y = 3. Then 3x + 6 = 12 → x = 2. Check: 6 − 12 = −6 ✓.

quiz.q: The sum of three consecutive integers is 72. What is the largest?

quiz.why: x(x − 5) = 0, so x = 0 or x = 5. Dividing by x loses the x = 0 solution.

quiz.q: Write x² + 8x + 5 in the form (x + p)² + q.
quiz.why: Half of 8 is 4: (x + 4)² = x² + 8x + 16, so subtract 16: (x + 4)² − 16 + 5 = (x + 4)² − 11.

quiz.q: What is the turning point of y = (x − 3)² + 2?
quiz.why: The bracket is zero when x = 3, giving the minimum y = 2. So (3, 2).

quiz.q: Solve x² − 2x − 4 = 0, giving answers to 2 decimal places.

quiz.why: −3x > 12. Dividing by −3 reverses the sign: x < −4.

quiz.q: List the integers n such that −3 ≤ 2n < 6.
quiz.why: Divide by 2: −1.5 ≤ n < 3. Integers: −1, 0, 1, 2 (3 is not included).

quiz.q: A region is below the line y = 2x + 1, and the line is drawn dashed. Which inequality describes it?
quiz.why: Below the line → y < …; dashed means the line is not included, so strict <.
Subtract 2x and add 7: 12 ≤ 3x, so 4 ≤ x, i.e. x ≥ 4.

quiz.q: A number line shows a filled circle at 2, an open circle at 5, and a line between them. Which inequality is this?
quiz.why: Filled at 2 → 2 is included (≤). Open at 5 → 5 is not included (<).

quiz.q: Make r the subject of A = πr².
quiz.why: Divide by π: r² = A/π. Then square root: r = √(A/π).

quiz.q: Make x the subject of y = (3x − 2)/5.

quiz.why: (x − 3)(x + 3) / [(x + 2)(x + 3)] = (x − 3)/(x + 2). Cancelling the x² terms (−9/(5x + 6)) is not allowed.

quiz.q: Make t the subject of a(t + 3) = bt.
quiz.why: at + 3a = bt → 3a = bt − at = t(b − a) → t = 3a/(b − a). Option C still has t on both sides.
Common denominator 2x: 2/(2x) + 1/(2x) = 3/(2x).
Difference 4 → 4n. First term 7 = 4 + 3, so 4n + 3.
Difference −3 → −3n. When n = 1, −3 + c = 20 → c = 23. So 23 − 3n.
Differences 7, 11, 15, 19; second difference 4 → 2n². Terms − 2n² = 0, 1, 2, 3, 4 = n − 1. So 2n² + n − 1. (n² + 4n − 3 only fits the first two terms.)
First term 3, ratio 2: 3 × 2ⁿ⁻¹. Check n = 1: 3 × 2⁰ = 3 ✓. 3 × 2ⁿ starts at 6.

quiz.q: Is 100 a term of the sequence with nth term 4n + 2?
options: No, because n = 24.5 is not a whole number
quiz.why: 4n + 2 = 100 → n = 24.5. Not a whole number, so 100 is not a term (all terms are 2 more than a multiple of 4).

examIntro: Paper 2 / Paper 4 style. [No calculator] questions are Paper 2; [Calculator] questions are Paper 4. Write full working first, then open the mark scheme: M1 = method mark, A1 = accuracy mark (correct answer from correct working), B1 = mark for a correct result on its own. Give yourself one mark per point you got.

exam.q: [No calculator] (a) Expand and simplify (x + 1)(x − 2)(2x + 3). (b) Factorise 6x² + x − 15.
[No calculator] Solve the simultaneous equations 3x + 4y = 5 and 5x − 2y = 17. Show all your working.
points: M1: correct method to eliminate a letter, e.g. 10x − 4y = 34 added to 3x + 4y = 5 (13x = 39)

exam.q: [No calculator] Solve the simultaneous equations y = x + 1 and x² + y² = 25.
[Calculator] Solve 3x² − 5x − 4 = 0. Show your working and give your answers correct to 2 decimal places.
[No calculator] A rectangle has length (x + 5) cm and width (x − 1) cm. Its area is 40 cm². (a) Show that x² + 4x − 45 = 0. (b) Solve the equation and hence find the perimeter of the rectangle.
points: A1: x = 5 (x = −9 rejected: the width would be negative)

exam.q: [No calculator] (a) Solve −5 < 3x + 1 ≤ 13. (b) List the integers that satisfy this inequality.

[No calculator] Region R satisfies y ≥ 1, x + y ≤ 6 and y ≤ 2x. (a) Find the coordinates of the three vertices of R. (b) Find the greatest value of 3x + y for a point (x, y) in R with integer coordinates.
points: B1: (5, 1) where y = 1 meets x + y = 6
B1: (2, 4) where x + y = 6 meets y = 2x
M1: evaluates 3x + y at points in R, e.g. (5, 1) → 16, (2, 4) → 10
exam.note: In the exam you would draw the three lines on a grid first; sketching them helps here too.

exam.q: [No calculator] Make h the subject of the formula V = ⅓πr²h.
[Calculator] Solve 3/(x + 1) + 2/(x − 2) = 1. Give your answers correct to 2 decimal places.
[No calculator] The sequence 1, 8, 27, 64, … continues. (a) Write down the next two terms. (b) Write down the nth term.
[No calculator] For the sequence 6, 11, 16, 21, … (a) find the nth term (b) find the 50th term.
[No calculator] The sequence 4, 11, 22, 37, 56, … is quadratic. (a) Find the nth term. (b) Which term of the sequence is 211?
